start.topic: AniCheck: a mobile app for rice leaf disease identification

question.question: Regarding your objective to provide a decision-support tool, how does an application that strictly excludes any data aggregation or transmission fulfill the broader goal of informing local agricultural advisory campaigns?

sources.text:

4. How acceptable is the developed application to its intended users when evaluated against the
ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics of functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability?
Objectives of the Study
The general objective was to develop and evaluate a mobile application capable of identifying
common rice leaf diseases without requiring an internet connection. Specifically, the study aimed to
assemble a labeled image dataset of rice leaves representing four disease classes and a healthy class;
to train a convolutional neural network on that dataset using transfer learning; to convert and embed
the trained model in an Android application with an interface suitable for users with limited formal
schooling; and to evaluate both the classification performance of the model and the acceptability of
the application to its intended users.
Scope and Limitations
The application identifies four disease classes — bacterial leaf blight, brown spot, leaf smut, and
tungro — plus a healthy class. These four were selected because they were the diseases most
frequently named by farmers during the initial interviews and because they present visible foliar
symptoms. Diseases whose symptoms appear principally on the panicle, stem, or root, including
sheath blight and false smut, are outside the coverage of the system.
The image dataset was collected exclusively within Barangay Masagana during a six-week window
in the 2024 wet season. The application runs on Android 9.0 and above; no iOS version was
produced. The system returns an identification and a confidence percentage; it does not recommend
a specific chemical product or dosage, since the proponents judged that prescribing agricultural
chemicals falls outside both the competence of the development team and the intended function of a
diagnostic aid. The application is intended as a decision-support tool and not as a replacement for
consultation with a qualified agricultural technician.
Significance of the Study
For smallholder farmers, the study offers a means of obtaining a preliminary disease identification at
the moment of observation rather than at the next available consultation. For agricultural extension
officers, a tool that handles routine identification may allow scarce technician time to be directed
toward the cases that genuinely require expert judgment. For the local government unit, the
aggregate pattern of identifications could in principle inform the targeting of advisory campaigns,
although the present version of the system does not transmit or aggregate any data. For future
researchers, the study contributes a documented dataset collection procedure and a baseline set of
results against which alternative architectures may be compared.

question.grounding_reference: For the local government unit, the aggregate pattern of identifications could in principle inform the targeting of advisory campaigns, although the present version of the system does not transmit or aggregate any data.

turns.answer: Informing advisory campaigns isn't one of our objectives. Our objectives on page 5 are to build the dataset, train the model with transfer learning, embed it in an offline Android app, and evaluate accuracy and acceptability. The advisory point appears only in Significance, and we worded it as something the aggregate pattern could do in principle. We kept the app fully on-device for two reasons in Chapter 1: mobile data coverage in Barangay Masagana is unreliable, so a server round-trip would fail exactly where farmers stand in the field, and keeping the identification history only on the farmer's own phone avoids collecting data about their farms without a consent process we haven't designed. Sending anonymous counts to the municipal agriculture office would be a separate study, with its own consent and data-handling design.

evaluation.primary_gap: The candidate narrowly interpreted 'objectives' as only the bulleted list on page 5, ignoring the logical tension between the stated purpose of the tool (as defined in Significance) and its technical implementation constraints.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate clarified that their defined research objectives are strictly technical/developmental, noting that the mention of informing agricultural campaigns is an auxiliary possibility mentioned in the Significance section rather than a functional requirement of the current prototype.

next_question.question: I see your rationale for the on-device storage constraint, but let's look at the sampling method used to validate this. You mention that respondents captured between three and five identifications on leaves available at the session; given that the model's reliability is being tested against these specific images, how can you ensure the leaves provided during these thirty-minute sessions offer enough morphological diversity to truly validate the model's accuracy, or are you just testing for usability here?

Evaluation Design
Model performance was evaluated on the 648-image test set using accuracy, precision, recall, and
F1-score computed per class, together with a confusion matrix.
System acceptability was evaluated using a survey instrument adapted from ISO/IEC 25010,
covering four characteristics: functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability. The
instrument consisted of twenty statements, five per characteristic, rated on a five-point Likert scale.
The instrument was translated into Filipino and reviewed for clarity by the adviser and by one
faculty member from the college.
Thirty respondents were selected through purposive sampling from among the rice farmers of
Barangay Masagana, the criteria being active cultivation of rice during the current season and
ownership of an Android smartphone. Each respondent attended a single session in which the
application was installed on their device, its use was demonstrated, and they were guided through
capturing between three and five identifications on leaves available at the session. Sessions ran
approximately thirty minutes. The survey was administered immediately afterward, with the
proponents reading each statement aloud and recording the response.
Responses were analyzed using weighted mean. The scale was interpreted according to the ranges in

Ethical Considerations
Permission to conduct the study within the barangay was obtained in writing from the barangay
captain. Participation was voluntary and respondents were informed that they could withdraw at any
point. Consent was obtained verbally at the start of each session, since several respondents indicated
discomfort with signing documents. No personally identifying information was recorded on the
survey forms, and the application stores identification history only on the user's own device.

turns.answer: You're right, and I conflated two different things. The 94.7% on page 11 comes from the 648-image test set, which was split from the same collection as the training set: detached leaves photographed flat on white cardboard between 8 and 10 AM, about 25 cm from the leaf. So it tells us the model separates the five classes under those controlled conditions, not that it holds up in the field. The session identifications were part of the acceptability survey, and we never scored them against a technician's label, so they don't validate accuracy at all. The honest claim is that field accuracy is untested. Closing that gap means a second test set of attached leaves photographed in the field at different times of day, labeled by the municipal technician, and reporting per-class recall on it, especially bacterial leaf blight, our weakest class at 0.813.

evaluation.primary_gap: The candidate lacks any quantitative evidence or baseline performance data for the model in uncontrolled, real-world conditions.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate acknowledges that the 94.7% accuracy metric is limited to controlled lab conditions and admits that field accuracy remains untested, proposing a future methodology to address this gap.

next_question.question: I appreciate the transparency regarding your error cases, but you mention the system cannot express multiple conditions while maintaining a single-class output. Since you acknowledge this architectural limitation, why did you conclude the system is a useful diagnostic tool when it is fundamentally unable to represent the diagnostic reality of comorbid leaf infections observed in the field?

Discussion
The overall accuracy of 94.7% is lower than the figures commonly reported in the plant disease
classification literature, where results above 99% on the PlantVillage dataset are routine. The
proponents attribute the difference principally to dataset scale: 3,240 images across five classes is an
order of magnitude smaller than the datasets on which those figures were obtained.
The acceptability results indicate that the intended users found the system usable and useful. The
gap between the usability rating and the reliability rating is instructive: respondents were more
confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them. For a
diagnostic tool this is the more consequential of the two dimensions, and it corresponds directly to
the per-class weakness identified on bacterial leaf blight.

next_question.grounding_reference: In several such instances the leaf in question carried symptoms of more than one condition, a case the present system cannot express since it returns a single class.

turns.answer: We didn't conclude that it's a diagnostic tool in that sense. The usefulness on page 13 is the respondents' acceptability rating, and our Conclusion on page 14 deliberately calls the system a preliminary decision-support aid that shouldn't replace a technician where a costly treatment follows. The single-class output is the reason for that wording: our Limitations say we never established its behaviour on a leaf with two conditions, and the error cases on page 13 show that's where respondents caught it out. So the claim is narrow. It gives a first identification at the moment of observation for the common single-disease case, with a confidence percentage. Our second recommendation addresses exactly your point: a way to express multiple simultaneous conditions, or an inconclusive result, instead of forcing one class.

evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate clarified that the system is positioned as a preliminary decision-support tool rather than a comprehensive diagnostic instrument, noting that they explicitly framed the system's narrow scope and acknowledged its limitations regarding multi-condition leaves in their conclusions and recommendations.

next_question.question: You concede that the field accuracy remains untested, yet your evaluation design claims to have measured the 'reliability' characteristic of the system via the ISO/IEC 25010 survey instrument. If the model's diagnostic performance is unproven in uncontrolled environments, how can you justify labeling the system as 'reliable' based solely on the subjective feedback of farmers who only tested the app under your immediate guidance during a single thirty-minute session?

turns.answer: The 4.09 is the respondents' perceived reliability, not a measurement of the model, and we report it that way. Our Limitations on page 14 say the evaluation came right after a guided session and measures initial impression rather than sustained use, with respondents from the same barangay that supplied the training images. Even under those favourable conditions reliability was the lowest-rated characteristic, below usability at 4.42, and we read that gap as the farmers telling us they weren't sure the answers were right, which matches the bacterial leaf blight recall of 0.813. That's why the conclusion stops at a preliminary aid. Measured reliability needs the two studies we recommend: the app's identifications compared against a technician on the same leaves, and farmers using it unsupervised across a full cropping season.

evaluation.primary_gap: The candidate admits the survey measures only initial perception but fails to address the inherent contradiction of using an ISO/IEC 25010 'reliability' metric when the underlying system performance remains unvalidated.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate clarifies that the 4.09 reliability score reflects subjective user perception during an initial guided session rather than objective system performance, and argues that this result, when contextualized alongside recall metrics and future research recommendations, serves as a preliminary aid rather than a definitive claim of system reliability.

You have successfully completed your defense session. Across the five turns of the examination, the panel steadily increased the difficulty of their inquiry, moving from an initial level of 2 to a sustained level of 3 in the final three turns. Your overall performance was particularly strong in clarity and grounding, where you achieved averages of 88 and 84, respectively, though your depth of response averaged 72.

One notable moment occurred during the second turn, where you faced significant pushback that escalated the difficulty. It is to your credit that you recovered effectively, as your answer quality improved significantly compared to the prior turn.

The panel identified several areas for your consideration. Dr. Al-Farsi noted that you interpreted your objectives too narrowly, overlooking the tension between your tool’s stated purpose and its technical constraints. Dr. Nguyen identified gaps regarding your methodology, specifically concerning your conflation of training accuracy with sampling rigor and the distinction between morphological diversity and geographic location. Furthermore, you lacked quantitative baselines for real-world conditions. Finally, Dr. O’Sullivan highlighted a contradiction in your work, noting that you applied an ISO/IEC 25010 reliability metric despite your system's lack of performance validation. While Dr. Schmidt offered no specific gaps, your cumulative feedback centers on the need to better align your technical implementations with your broader project objectives and methodological rigor.

Our second recommendation addresses exactly your point: a way to express multiple simultaneous conditions, or an inconclusive result, instead of forcing one class.

evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate clarified that the system is positioned as a preliminary decision-support tool rather than a comprehensive diagnostic instrument, noting that they explicitly framed the system's narrow scope and acknowledged its limitations regarding multi-condition leaves in their conclusions and recommendations.

transcript.question: You concede that the field accuracy remains untested, yet your evaluation design claims to have measured the 'reliability' characteristic of the system via the ISO/IEC 25010 survey instrument. If the model's diagnostic performance is unproven in uncontrolled environments, how can you justify labeling the system as 'reliable' based solely on the subjective feedback of farmers who only tested the app under your immediate guidance during a single thirty-minute session?

Evaluation Design
Model performance was evaluated on the 648-image test set using accuracy, precision, recall, and
F1-score computed per class, together with a confusion matrix.
System acceptability was evaluated using a survey instrument adapted from ISO/IEC 25010,
covering four characteristics: functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability. The
instrument consisted of twenty statements, five per characteristic, rated on a five-point Likert scale.
The instrument was translated into Filipino and reviewed for clarity by the adviser and by one
faculty member from the college.
Thirty respondents were selected through purposive sampling from among the rice farmers of
Barangay Masagana, the criteria being active cultivation of rice during the current season and
ownership of an Android smartphone. Each respondent attended a single session in which the
application was installed on their device, its use was demonstrated, and they were guided through
capturing between three and five identifications on leaves available at the session. Sessions ran
approximately thirty minutes. The survey was administered immediately afterward, with the
proponents reading each statement aloud and recording the response.
Responses were analyzed using weighted mean. The scale was interpreted according to the ranges in

Ethical Considerations
Permission to conduct the study within the barangay was obtained in writing from the barangay
captain. Participation was voluntary and respondents were informed that they could withdraw at any
point. Consent was obtained verbally at the start of each session, since several respondents indicated
discomfort with signing documents. No personally identifying information was recorded on the
survey forms, and the application stores identification history only on the user's own device.

transcript.grounding_reference: System acceptability was evaluated using a survey instrument adapted from ISO/IEC 25010, covering four characteristics: functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability.
transcript.answer: The 4.09 is the respondents' perceived reliability, not a measurement of the model, and we report it that way. Our Limitations on page 14 say the evaluation came right after a guided session and measures initial impression rather than sustained use, with respondents from the same barangay that supplied the training images. Even under those favourable conditions reliability was the lowest-rated characteristic, below usability at 4.42, and we read that gap as the farmers telling us they weren't sure the answers were right, which matches the bacterial leaf blight recall of 0.813. That's why the conclusion stops at a preliminary aid. Measured reliability needs the two studies we recommend: the app's identifications compared against a technician on the same leaves, and farmers using it unsupervised across a full cropping season.

evaluation.primary_gap: The candidate admits the survey measures only initial perception but fails to address the inherent contradiction of using an ISO/IEC 25010 'reliability' metric when the underlying system performance remains unvalidated.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate clarifies that the 4.09 reliability score reflects subjective user perception during an initial guided session rather than objective system performance, and argues that this result, when contextualized alongside recall metrics and future research recommendations, serves as a preliminary aid rather than a definitive claim of system reliability.
